source_metadata.title: Explicit, Not Longer: What Makes Epistemic Stance Survive Memory Compression
source_metadata.input_file: Explicit, Not Longer What Makes Epistemic Stance Survive Memory Compression - 2608.06953v1.pdf

atoms.canonical_statement: The study tested whether epistemic stance survives memory compression better when the same stance is represented as a labelled field rather than as parenthetical prose.

source_anchor.sentence: Paragraph beginning “The hypothesis, and what happened to it.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The study further decomposed the field-versus-prose format to determine which properties—labels, bracketing, wording, layout, or length—contribute to stance retention and whether those effects transfer across models.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 7 opening paragraphs describing the six-form ablation.

atoms.canonical_statement: Sixty synthetic claims across seven registers were each written in two matched forms carrying the identical assertion and stance content: a labelled-field form and a parenthetical-prose form.
For each claim, pressure level, and replicate, the field and prose arms received the same compressor prompt, settings, filler notes, and target position; the random seed did not depend on the arm.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 4 paragraph beginning “Both go to the same compressor.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The 60-claim headline runs used the BRUTAL budget of eight notes compressed to at most 25 words and the SEVERE budget of eight notes compressed to at most 12 words, with three replicates per claim.

source_anchor.sentence: Pressure discussion and paragraph beginning “The claim is the unit that generalises.”

atoms.canonical_statement: A blind reader saw only the stored memory and the claim to look up, never the source note, arm, or pressure level, and classified the claim as established fact, qualified, or absent.

Statistical inference treated the claim as the generalization unit, using a claim-clustered bootstrap and an exact sign test over per-claim differences rather than pair-level tests on correlated replicates.

source_anchor.sentence: Paragraph beginning “The claim is the unit that generalises.”

atoms.canonical_statement: An assumption-light permutation check shuffled the arm label within each claim over 20,000 permutations.

The held-out replication used 60 newly written claims following the same seven-register specification, with the prediction and decision rule committed publicly before any model call; it ran on Haiku 4.5 with one run, three replicates, and two budgets.

The ablation compared six note forms—explicit sentences, labelled fields, unbracketed promoted prose, padded parenthetical prose, unlabelled own-line form, and parenthetical prose—while holding claims, budgets, seeds, replicates, fillers, and positions fixed.

A deterministic no-model gate was used as an additional readout for the two-cell and ablation results, with the authors treating its open-class stance-recognition limits as a reason to interpret its magnitudes as lower bounds.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 6 “A readout with no model in it.”

atoms.canonical_statement: A stratified sample of 50 stored memories from 40 distinct claims across both models and both arms was hand-labelled by the paper author under condition blinding, using the same three-way outcome question as the model judge.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 6 “And fifty items a human read.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The released record checker applies three field-level rules: detectable source hedging must not map to asserted certainty, named speakers require a nonempty SOURCE field, and dated claims require a nonempty AS_OF field; missing retention fields are classified as malformed.

A pilot attempting to localize stance loss was unresolved: a write-time gate flagged 9 of 10 source-to-note transitions and 1 of 10 note-to-memory transitions, while hand review found a stance cue in 9 of 10 notes.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 3 paragraph beginning “Where the loss happens is not obvious.”

atoms.canonical_statement: A prose-repair pilot fired on 8 of 10 notes, increased input tokens by 23.4%, and changed the final stored-memory verdict on none of the 10 cases, with 0 recovered and 0 broken.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 3 “Repairing the prose does not survive.”

atoms.canonical_statement: An early blind-reader parser bug discarded about 6% of then-existing verdicts non-randomly and inflated the pooled field advantage from +4.0 percentage points after the fix to +9.3 points before the fix; the repaired parser later recovered 33 of 4,104 replies with none unusable.

On Haiku 4.5, labelled fields increased stance retention by 15.83 percentage points versus parenthetical prose (30.3% vs 14.4%), with a claim-clustered 95% CI of +10.8 to +20.6 points; 37 claims favored fields, 2 favored prose, and 21 tied.

atoms.canonical_statement: Within-claim permutation testing placed the observed mean field-minus-prose difference beyond every one of 20,000 shuffled values on both models, giving p = 0.00005, the test resolution floor.

On the earlier 10-claim office-work corpus, the same two budgets yielded only +3.7 points on Haiku and +3.7 points on Sonnet with claim-clustered intervals containing zero, demonstrating that the narrow corpus had produced a false null and a false model-family moderator.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 4 “Ten claims said the opposite, on the same models.”

atoms.canonical_statement: At the BRUTAL budget on Haiku, labelled-field memories retained stance 44% of the time, stored the claim as bare fact 11%, and evicted it 45%; parenthetical prose retained stance 21%, stored bare fact 28%, and evicted 52%.
On Sonnet 4.5 pooled across both hard budgets, claim eviction was statistically indistinguishable between field and prose forms (129 vs 123 of 360; p = 0.52).

atoms.canonical_statement: Haiku’s pooled +15.8-point stance advantage decomposed into 28 fewer bare-fact stores and 29 fewer evictions in the field arm, so roughly half of the gain operated through better claim retention rather than qualification alone.

The field effect was positive on both models in six of seven registers; project claims showed the largest mean effects (+0.21 Haiku, +0.23 Sonnet), while conflict claims were weakest (+0.12 Haiku and approximately zero Sonnet).
At the SEVERE budget, 43 of 60 Haiku claims tied because both arms often lost the claim entirely; nevertheless, each hard budget remained significant when analyzed separately on both models.
Claims with disagreeing sources were a concentrated failure mode for the single-slot schema: three of the six worst claim-level cases across the two models involved source conflict.

The preregistered Haiku 4.5 replication reproduced the field advantage at +15.55 percentage points (28.61% vs 13.06%), with a claim-clustered 95% CI of +11.4 to +20.0; 38 claims favored fields and 1 favored prose.

atoms.canonical_statement: The no-model ablation readout preserved the direction of five of seven contrasts on both models but reversed the sign of the length contrast; its labels contrast was −1.1 on Haiku and +0.3 on Sonnet, consistent with the gate being unable to recognize some field-label values.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 7 “The same contrasts, scored by an instrument with no model in it.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The study did not detect a retention difference between labelled fields and explicit full-sentence prose on either model, but the available interval was too wide to establish equivalence.

In an end-to-end pilot on one model, writing notes to the schema before compression increased clean writes from 3 of 10 to 7 of 10; when the schema was filled, all four fields were complete in 10 of 10 records.
In that same 10-case pilot, the model classified 8 of 10 sources as something other than plainly asserted: six as rumor and two as hedged.

A prose detector scored schema-to-schema memories as clean in 5 of 10 cases versus 7 of 10 when the same schema note was compressed to prose, even though inspection found all four schema fields intact in 10 of 10 cases, demonstrating an instrument mismatch rather than poorer record retention.
The authors conclude that epistemic stance should be made explicit in memory writes rather than merely made longer, because length padding did not improve retention on either evaluated model.
The authors conclude that labelled fields are a reproducible contributor to stance retention across both evaluated models, while the contribution of wording and bracketing is model-dependent.
The authors decline to name a single mechanism because the two models show nearly identical net field effects but different ablation decompositions.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 7 paragraph beginning “We are deliberately not naming a single mechanism.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The labelled schema retains an implementation advantage even when explicit prose may retain stance similarly: a program can directly check whether required stance and provenance fields are present without recognizing open-class stance wording.

source_anchor.sentence: Section 10 paragraph describing the schema’s remaining advantage.

atoms.canonical_statement: The main experiments used only Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4.5 from one provider, so the evaluated models are not a representative sample of memory compressors.

The stimuli were 60 hand-written synthetic English claims in seven registers with stance-free fillers and exactly matched arms, which improves control but limits ecological validity for real memory systems that generate their own notes.
The reported field advantage is concentrated at the tight end of the pressure ladder; at looser budgets the effect is small and is not claimed.
The ablation is a sequential chain rather than a full factorial design, so interactions among labels, bracketing, wording, layout, and length were not measured.

source_anchor.sentence: Limitations — “The ablation is a chain, not a factorial.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The human check used only one annotator, who was the paper author and therefore blind to condition but not to the study hypothesis; no inter-rater agreement could be reported.

source_anchor.sentence: Limitations — “One human read fifty of these.”

atoms.canonical_statement: A single SOURCE field cannot naturally represent multiple disagreeing attributions, and conflict claims were a measured weak point; a multi-attribution schema was proposed but not tested.

source_anchor.sentence: Limitations — “What the schema still cannot do.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The checker can verify field presence and catch some detectable source-to-field inconsistencies, but it cannot generally detect a field that is present yet confidently filled with the wrong epistemic value; source-side stance detection remains limited by deterministic English lexicons.

source_anchor.sentence: Limitations — “What the schema still cannot do.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The end-to-end schema pipeline result is only a 10-case, one-model pilot and is not used as support for the paper’s main conclusion.

The authors released the experimental harness, scorer, figure script, paper source, every raw run, superseded runs with explanations, and the hand-annotation materials in the public collapseindex/factwash repository.

The paper’s reproducibility guard re-derives load-bearing numerical claims from summary JSON and includes tests that intentionally break the paper in 48 ways to verify that the consistency checker fires.

extraction_limitations: The source is an AI/ML preprint using synthetic claims and model-based readouts; extraction records what the paper reports and does not externally verify the experiments.
Pilot and withdrawn or instrument-dependent findings are preserved only when explicitly identified as such; retracted mechanisms are not converted into positive evidence atoms.

The current LiteratureAtom schema has no dedicated fields for preregistration status, multi-instrument validation, or retracted-claim ledgers, so those details are represented in canonical statements and tags.
Some percentage-point differences for eviction were calculated from source-reported raw counts and are marked calculated_from_reported_data.
